title: National Insurance on partnership profits
headline: Partners in LLPs pay no employer NICs. CenTax’s equivalent charge: £1.9bn.
description: A partner in a law, accountancy or medical partnership pays Class 4 National Insurance on their profits, but no equivalent of the 15% employer charge that falls on an employee’s pay. The Centre for the Analysis of Taxation calls this an accident of history and models a charge equivalent to employer National Insurance on partnership profits, with a partnership allowance matching the £10,500 employment allowance. It puts the yield at £1.9 billion in 2026-27 after behavioural responses, down from a static £2.4 billion. This card takes that figure and grows it with the OBR’s National Insurance forecast.

baselinePolicy.text: Partners pay Class 4 National Insurance at 6% on profits between £12,570 and £50,270 and 2% above; no equivalent of the 15% employer charge falls on partnership profits.

source.quote: partnership does not pay any equivalent of Employer NICs

alreadyIncludes: Employer National Insurance at 15% from April 2025 (Autumn Budget 2024, Table 5.1 line 26).

terms.label: CenTax’s estimate for Partnership NICs at the employer rate with a £10,500 partnership allowance, after behaviour

source.quote: Levying ‘Partnership NICs’ would raise an estimated £1.9 billion in 2026-27, after accounting for behavioural responses and interactions with other taxes

rawSource.note: CenTax’s 2026-27 figure, grown with the OBR’s National Insurance receipts to the other years. The design is the researchers’: an employer-rate charge on partnership profits with a partnership allowance equal to the employment allowance.

caveats: CenTax’s central figure takes a fifth off a static £2.4 billion for behaviour; at a higher elasticity the yield falls further. Nobody in government has adopted the design or certified the number.
Grown with the OBR’s National Insurance forecast from 2026-27, which is our step.
Employer-side, so outside the manifesto lock on the government’s 2024 reading; a partner would call it a rise in their National Insurance, and the reading is contested.

considerations.text: CenTax reduces the static yield by 20% for partners who incorporate, retire, move or restructure their pay; that response is inside the £1.9 billion, and a larger one would take more.

sources.quote: after accounting for behavioural responses and interactions with other taxes

considerations.text: Almost half the revenue would come from partners in the top 0.1% of earners, and only about a third of partners would pay anything because of the allowance.

sources.quote: Almost half the revenue raised from introducing Partnership NICs would be raised from partners in the top 0.1%

considerations.text: The 2024 Budget treated employer National Insurance as outside the manifesto’s promise not to increase National Insurance. A charge equivalent to it on partnership profits follows that reading, and the reading is contested.

sources.quote: we will not increase National Insurance

interactions.text: CenTax’s charge mirrors the 15% employer rate; the £1.9 billion is at that rate, and moving the employer rate would move this too.
Class 4 is what partners pay today. Raising it and adding Partnership NICs stacks two charges on the same profits.
